chunks: "I'd read 'symmetrical' as two identical FETs, same type and same size, in the half bridge.
The pros are that it's simple and flexible: one part number, the same gate-drive design on both sides, and the bridge is naturally bidirectional, so you can run it as a buck or a boost.
It's the natural choice at 50% duty, and for inverters, motor drives and bidirectional chargers. The con is that in a buck the two FETs do different jobs.
The high side conducts only for D and does all the hard switching; the low side conducts for 1-D but switches nearly for free because its body diode clamps the node first.
So if D is small, like 12 volts down to 1. 2 volts, the low side runs hot with 90% of the conduction loss while the high side is mostly idle silicon.
For a fixed total area the optimum has conductance split as square root of D to square root of 1-D , which for D equals 0.
1 means a high side three times the resistance of the low side and 20% less conduction loss.
Plus you'd want the high side optimized for low Q gd and the low side for low R DS(on) . So symmetry costs efficiency and thermal balance unless the duty is near 50%."
